S.O. 936.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the 
proviso to article 309 of the Constitution, the President 
hereby directs that the Lt. Governor, Andaman and Nicobar 
Islands shall exercise the powers lo make Rules in regard 
to the Central Civil Services and Posts in Gronn ‘A’ and 
‘B’ the maximum of which docs not exceed Rs. 2-,000|-, under 
his administrative control. 


2, Any Recruitment Rules, including anv Rule relating to 
probation, confirmation, senioritv and promotion made in 
pursuance of this direction shall be subject to previous con¬ 
sultation with the Union Public Service Commission. 


3. Tn case of a post, appoint to which requires the nrior 
approval of the Central Government, prior approval of Cent¬ 
ral Government shall be obtained also in respect of the Re¬ 
cruitment Rules for such posts, in addition to the previous 
consultation with the Union Public Service Commission re¬ 
garding such Recruitment Rules,

New Delhi, the 17th January, 1985 
INCOME-TAX 

S.O. 939.—It is hereby notified for general information 
that the Institution mentioned below has been approved by 
Department of Science Technology, New Delhi, the prescribed 
authority for the purposes of clause (ii) of sub-section (1) of 
section 35 of the Income-tax Act, 196l read with Rule 6 of 
the Income-tax Rules, 1962 under the Category “Association" 
subject to the following conditions ;— 

(i) That the Tmala Cancer Research Centre Society 

will maintain a separate account of the sums receiv¬ 
ed by it for scientific research. 

(ii) That the 6ai(J Society will furnish annual returns of 

its scientific research activities to tbe Prescribed 
Authority for every financial year in such forms as 
may be laid down and intimated to them for this 
purpose by 30th April each year. 

(iii) That the said Association will submit to the Pres¬ 

cribed Authority by 30th June each year a copy of 
their audited annual accounts showing their total 
income and expenditure and balance sheet showing 
its assets liabilities with a copy of each Of these 
documents to the concerned Cotnmissioner of 
Income-tax. 

INSTITUTION 

Amala Cancer Research Centre Society, Trichur. 

This notification is effective for a period from 20-11-84 to 
31-3-86. 

[No. 6111/F. No. 203/190/84-rrA-U]

ORDER 

S.O, 963.—^Whereas the Central Government is of opinion 
that it is necessary and expedient so to do for the deve¬ 
lopment of the export trade of India that in exercise of the 
powers conferred by section 6 of the Export (Quality Con¬ 
trol and Inspection) Act, 1963 (22 of 1963), the Vacuum 
Flasks shall be subject to quality control and inspection 
prior to export; 







‘ «nT?T'FT7nrTO-. jtH 9, 

And whereas the Central Oovemment has formulated the 
proposals specified below for the said purpose and has for¬ 
warded the same to the txport Inspection Council as rc- 
qu'red by sub-rule (2) of rule 11 of the Export (Quality 
Control and Inspection) Rules, 19(54; 

Now, therefore, in pursuance of the said sub-rule, and 
in supersession of the notiflcation No, S.O. 1616, dated the 
7fh -May, 1968, the Central Government hereby published 
the said proposals for the information of the public likely 
to be alfectbd thereby. 

2. Not'ce is hereby given that any person dosifing to for¬ 
ward any objections or suggestions with respect to the said 
proposals may forward the same within forty-five days of 
the date of publication of this order in the Official Gazette 
to-the Export Inspection Council, of India, 11th Floor. 
Pragati Tower, 26, Rajeiidra Place, New Delhi-110008, ther¬ 
mal shock If the number of defectives found in the sample 
is less than Or equal to the corresponding acceptance num¬ 
ber given in column 8 of Table 2. 

proposals 

(i) To notify that Vacuum Flasks shall be Subject to 
quality control and inspection prior to export; 

Oi) To specify the type of quality control and inspection 
in accordance with the draft Export of Vacuum 
Flasks (Quality Control and Inspection) Rules, 
1984 set out In ' Annexure-ll to this order as the 
type of, inspection which shall be applied to such 
Vacuum Flasks prior to export; 


(iil) To recognise:— 

(a) relevant Indian Standard or any other national 
standard; 

(b) contractual specifications subject to the product 
specifying the minimum of the characteristics 
specified in Annexure-I to this order ; ' 

(c) the specifications declared by the exporter to be 
the agreed specifications , of the expoTt contract 
between the foreign buyer and'the exporter, for 
such export contracts as are confirmed prior to 
the date of publication of this order in the Offi¬ 
cial Gazette and exported within a period of sixty 
days from that date; as the standard specifications 
for vacuum flasks. 


(iv) To prohibit the export in the course of international 
trade of vacuum flasks unless the same is either ac-- 
companled by a certificate of inspectlfin issu^ by 
any of the Export Inspection Agencies established 
under section 7 of the Export (Quality Control and 
Inspection) Act, 1963 (22 of l963), to the effect 
that the Vacuum ‘ Flasks are export-worthy in ac¬ 
cordance with the Export Of Vacuum Rasks 
(Quality Control and Inspection) Rules, 1984.

‘SPECIEICATIONSjFOR VACUUM BLASKS’ 

A. Specifications for refills 

1. The size, shape and -Ihe capacity of the refills shall be 
as agreed to between the buyer and the seller. 

2 . The refills shall be made of well annealeidglass and shall 
have smooth surface. 

3. The silvering shall be uniform tmd free from flakes. 

4. The spacers, if any, shall not be loose. 

5. The thermal shock resistance of the refill shall bo 
considered adequate if the refill suffers no damage when 
subjected to the following test; 

Ponr water at 27° rtr 2°C upto the neck of the refills and 
allow to stand for 3 minutes. Empty therefill and pour boil¬ 
ing water (100°C) immediately and allow to stand for 3^ 
minutes. Empty the refill and pour water at 27° i 2°C 
Immediately and allow to stand for 3 minutes. The time for 
pouring water in and out Shall not exceed 15 second In 
each case.

3. Nothing in this order shall apply to the export by sea, 
land or air of samples of Vacuum Flasks not exceeding 
Rs. 125.00 only in Free on Board value to the prospective 
buyers. 

4. in thiainotjfioaflon, ‘Vacuum Flasks’ means:— 

(i) Any composite container consisting of an outer pro¬ 

tective case provided with a closure and suitable 
means for its carrying. The Outer case shall house 
a stoppered double Walled glass container (called 
the refill): wfth the walls silvered and the space 
in between maintained'under vabuum to reduce to 
a minimum the transfer Of heat to and from the 
contents placed in it. 

(ii) Refills meant for the said vacuum flasks.

ween the purchaser and the supplier, brimful capacities of

7.1 The brinjful capacity of sizes other than mentioned 
above shall be as agreed to between the exporter and foreign

8. Specification for the outer components of Vacuum 
riasks. 

8.1 Materials 

tal Outer Protective case and Accessories—Outer pro- 
teaive cases and accessories shall be of materials 
which shall be rigid enough to hold the refill se¬ 
curely under conditions of use and protect it from 
damage in normal handling. 

' (b) The stopper of the refill shall be non-toxic, corro¬ 
sion-resistant and durable. When fitted to the refill 
it shall not slip off and shall provide a leak-proof 
fitting. 

(c) The auxiliary closure (s), also intended for use as 
drinking cup(s). shall be non-toxic, corrosion-re¬ 
sistant and shall not deform under normal condi¬ 
tions of use. 

(d) The outer protective case, auxiliary closures and 
other components of vacuum finsks shall be as 
agreed to between the buyers and seller. 

fc) The thickness of the tin plate shall in no case be 
less than 0.27 mm. 

8.2 Workmansh'p and Finish 

(a) The outer protective case shall hold the refill se¬ 
curely by suitable supporting components at the 
base and the neck. 

(b) The component holding the neck of the refill shall 
be so designed as to prevent entry of any liquid 
into the space in between the protective case and 
the refill. 

(c) The ring and bottom of the. protective case if 

made out of tin shall be.lacquered on both sides 
Z, and the body lacquered on the Inside only for pro¬ 
tection against corrosion. The body shall be suit¬ 
ably painted and varnished to protect the outs'de 
decoration. 

Note.—^The protective case may also be made Of 
materials other than tinplate provided they satisfy 
the requirements mentioned above. 

(d) Suitable handle or arrangement for suspension may 
be provided on a vacuum flask. 

(c) There shall be no objectionable scratches -on the 
decoration. 

(f) The base of vacuum flasks shall be stable so as to 
prevent tipping. 

8.3 I.eak-Proofness.—^The stopper both ‘push in’ IVpe and 
the ‘screw on’ type should fit snugly in the neck of the con¬ 
tainer so that it shall be leak proof. 

Assembled vacuum flask with refill half-filled with cold 
water and stoppered, when inverted and shaken well tor one 
minnte, shall not show any leakage of water. 

ANNEXURE-II 

Draft rules proposed to be made under section 17 of the 
Export (Quality Control and Inspection) Act. 1963 (22 of 
1963);— 

1. Short title and commencement—^These rules may be 
called the Export of Vacuum Flasks (Quality Control and 
inspection) Rules, 1984. 

2. Definitions.—In these rules, unless the context other- 
vise requires:— 

(a) “Act" means the Export (Quality Control and Ins¬ 
pection) Act, 1963 (22 of 1963); 

(b) “Agency’’ means any of the Export Inspection 
Agene'es established under section 7 of the Act; 

(c) “Council" means Export Inspection Council estab¬ 
lished under section 3 of the Act; 


19S5/PHALGUNA 18, 1906 


(d) Vacuum Flask means:— 

(i) Any composite container consisting of an outer 

protective case provided with a closure and spit- 
able means for its carrying The outer ca# 
shall house a stoppered double walled glass con¬ 
tainer (called the refill); with the walls silvered 
and the space in between maintained under va¬ 
cuum to reduce to a mmimum the transfer of 
heat to and from the contents placed In it. 

(ii) refills meant for the said Vacuum Flasks; 

(e) “Schedule" means the Schedule appended to these 

rules. 

3. Ba.sis of inspection.—Inspection of Vacuum Flasks shall 
be carried out with a view to ensure that the qualify of 
the same conforms to the specifications recognised by the 
Central Government under section 6 of the Act, namely:— 

(a) relevant Indian Standard or any other national 

standard; 

(b) Contractual specifications snbjeot to the product 
specifying the minimum of the characteristics shed- 
fled in Annexure-I to this order; 

(c) the specifications declared by the exporter to be 
the agreed specifications Of the export contract 
between the foreign buyer and the exporter, for 
.such export contracts as are confirmed prior to the 
date of publication of this order in the official 
gazette and exported within a period of sixty days 
from the date, as the standard specifications for 
vacuum flasks. 

either 

(a) By ensuring that the products have been manufac- 
tttred by exercising necessary inprocess quality 
control as specified In Appendlx-A, 

or 

(b) On the bas’s of the inspection and testing carried 
out in the manner specified in Appendix-B, 

4. Procedure of Inspection.—(1) An exporter intending to 
export a consignment of vacuum flasks/rdills shall give an 
intimation in writing to the agency furnishing therein details 
of the contractual specifications alongwlth a copy of the ex¬ 
port contract or order or letter of Credit to enable the 
agency to carry out inspection in accordance with rule 3. 

(2) For export of vacuum flasks/refills manufactured by 
exercis'ng adequate inprocess quality control as laid down tn 
Appendix ’A’ and the manufacturing unit adjudged as having 
adequate inprocess quality control drills by the Panel of 
Experts constituted by the Agency for this purpose, the ex¬ 
porter shall also submit alongwith the intimation mentioned 
in sub-rule (1) a declaration that the consignment of vacuum 
flasks or refills, as the case may be. intended for export has 
been manufactured by exercising adequate quality control 
as laid down in Appendix ‘A’ and that the consignment 
conforms to the standard specifications recognised for the 
purpose. 

f3) The exporter shall furnish to the agency the identi¬ 
fication mark applied on the consignment to be exported, 

(4) Every intimation Under sub-rule (11 shall be given not 
less than seven days prior to the despatch of the consign¬ 
ment from the manufacturer’s premfses and the intimation 
alongwith the declaration under sub-rule (21 shall be given 
not less than three days prior to the despatch of the con¬ 
signment’ from the manufacturer’s premises. 

(5) On receipt of the intimation nndet sub-rule (1) and 
the declaration, if any, under sub-rnlc (2), the agency:— 

(a) (i) On satisfying itself, that during the process of 
manufacture, the manufacturer hqd exercised ade¬ 
quate nuality control as laid down in Appendix ‘A.’ 
and followed the instructions, if any. issued by the 
Agency/Council in this regard to manufacture the 
product to conform to the standard specifications 
recognised for -ihe purpose shall, within three davs. 
issue a certificate declaring the consignment of va¬ 
cuum flask/refills as exportworthy;

(ii) In case where the manufacturer is not the exporter, 

however, the consignment shall be physically veri¬ 
fied and such verification and inspection as is neces¬ 
sary shall be carried out by the agency to ensure 
that the above conditions are complied with; 

(iii) The Agency shall, however, conduct spot checks of 

some of the consignments meant for export and 
also visit the units at regular intervals to verify 
the maintenance of the adequacy of improcess 
quality control drills adopted by the unit. 

(iv) If the manufacturing unit is found not adopting the 
required quality control measures at any stage of 
manufacture or does not comply with the recom¬ 
mendations of the Council or Agency, the unit shall 
be declares as not having adequate inprocess quality 
control drills, and in such cases the unit if so de¬ 
sires shall apply afresh for adjudgement of the 
maintenance of adequacy of in-process quality con¬ 
trol drills. 

(b) In case where the exporter has not declared under 
sub-rule (2) that adequate quality control as laid 
down in Appendix ‘A’ had been exercised, on satis¬ 
fying itself that the consignment of vacuum flasfls/ 
refills conform to the standard specifications re¬ 
cognised for the purpose, on the basis of inspection / 
testing carried out as laid down in Appendix ‘P' 
Or on the basis of both, shall within seven days of 
carrying out such inspection is.sue a certificate dc- 
cinring the consignment of vacuum flasks/rcfills ns 
exportworthy; 

Provided that where the agency is not so satis¬ 
fied. it shall refuse to issue a certificate to the ex¬ 
porter declaring the consignment of Vacuum Flasks/ 
refills as exportworthy and shall communicate such 
refusal within seven days to Ihc exporter along- 
with the reasons therefor. 

(c) (1) In case where the manufacturer is not the ex¬ 
porter under sub-rule (5) (a) or consignment is ins¬ 
pected under sub-rule (5) (b) the Agency shall, 
immediately after completion of the inspection, seal 
the packages in the consignment in the manner so 
as to ensure that the sealed cackages cannot be 
tampered with, 

(ii) Tn case of rejection of the conslyrnment, if the ex¬ 
porter so desires the consignment may not be seal¬ 
ed by the Agency but in such cases, however, the 
exporter shall not be entitled to prefer any appeal 
against the rejection, 

5. Place of Inspection.—^Every Inspection under these 
rules shall be carried out either (a) at the premises of the 
manufacturer of such products, or (b) .it the premises at 
which the goods are offered by the exporter, provided ade¬ 
quate facilities for inspection exists therein, 

6. Inspection Fee.—^Inspection Fee shall be paid by the 
exporter to the Agency as under :— 

(i) fa) For exports under inprocess quality control 
scheme at the rate of 0.2 per cent of the F.O.B. 
value subject to minimum of Rs. 20 per consign¬ 
ment. 

(b) For exports under consignmentwise inspection at 
the rate of 0,4 per cent of'the F.O.B. value sub¬ 
ject to a minimum of Rs. 20 per consignment. 

(li) Subject to a minimum of Rs. 20/- tier consignment 
the rate shall be 0,18 per cent anj 0.36 per cent 
for (a) and (b) respectively, for manufacturers/ 
exporters who are registered as Small Scale Manu¬ 
facturing Units with the concerned Governments of 
State/Union Territories. 

7. Appeal.—(1) Any person aggrieved by the refusal of 
the Agenev ‘‘o issue a certificate under sub-rule (S) of rule 
4, may within ten days of the receipt of the communication 
of such refusal by him, prefer an appeal to a Panel of Ex¬ 
perts consisting of not less than three but not more than 
seven persons appointed for the purpose by the Central 
Government,

(2) The Panel shall consist of atlsast two thirds of non- 
oHicials of the total membership of the Panel of Hxpetts. 

(3) The qu'j.Lim for the Panel shall be three. 

(4) The appeal shall be d sposed of within fifteen days of 
its receipt.

Quality Control.—The Quality Control of the Vacuum 
Flasks/rcfills shall be ensured by the manuf.tcturer by effect¬ 
ing the following controls at dift'erent stages of nianufac- 
tme, preservation and packing of the products as laid down 
below together with levels of controls as set out in the 
schedule appended thereto. 

(i) Purchase spec fleatious and raw materials control;— 

(a) Purchase specifications shall be laid down by the 
manufacturer incorporating the properties of raw 
materials to be used, 

(b) Either the accepted consignments shall be »o- 
■ companied by a supplier’s, test jtnd inspection 

certificate corroborating the requirements of the 
purchase specifications, in which case occasional 
checks shall be conducted at least once in 10 
consignments by the purchaser for a particular 
supplier to verity the correctness of the aforesaid 
lest or inspection certificates or the purchased 
mateiial shall be regularly tested and inspected 
cither in the laboratory within the factory or in 
an outside laboratory or test houses, 

let The sampling for inspection or tes- to be carried 
out shall be based on the recorded investigation. 

(d) After the inspection or test is curried out, syste¬ 
matic methods shall be adopted in segregating 
the accepted and rejected materials and for dis¬ 
posal ot the rejected materials. 

(e) Adequate records in respect of the aforesaid con¬ 

trols shall be regularly and systematically mafn- 
tamed by the manufacturer. 

(ii) Procc.ss Control: 

fa) Detailed process specifications shall be laid down 
by the mamifucturer for different stages of manu¬ 
facture. 

(b) Equipment and instrumentation facilities shall be 
adequate to contiol the process as laid down in 
the process specifications. 

(c) Adequate records shall be maintained by the 
manufacluicr to ensure the possibility of verl- 
fjdng the controls exercised during the process 
of the manufacture. 

(Iii) Piodiict Control 

(a) The manufacturer shall have cither his own test¬ 
ing facilities or shall bavc access to such testing 

facilities existing elsewhere to check up whether 
the product conforms to specifications recognis¬ 
ed under section 6 of the Act. 

(b) Sampling for test and inspection to be can ed out 
shall be based on the recorded investigation. 

(c) Adequate records in respect of sampling and 
test carried out shall be regularly and systemati¬ 
cally maintained. 

(d) The minimum levels of control to check the pro¬ 

ducts shall be as specified in schedule. 

fiv) Preservation Control.—The products shall he well 
preserved' both during the storage and the transit. 

(v) Packing Control.—The packages shall have a good 
presentability and sufficient strength to stand hand¬ 
ling during transit..

laying pipeline:

user in the lands specified in the .schedule appended to this 
notification;

section (1) of the Section 6 of the salj Act, the Central

lands specified in the schedule appended to this notification 
hereby acquired for laying the pipeline; 

And further in exercise of power conferred by sub-section 
(4) of that section, the Central Government directs that the 
right of user In the said lands shall instead of vesting in 
Central Government vests on this date of the publication of 
this declaration in the Gas Authority of India free from 
encumbrances.

S.O. 978.—Whereas it appears to the Central Government 
that it is necessary in the public interest that lor the trans¬ 
port of petroleum from Bijaipiir (M.P.) to Sawai Madhopur 
in Rajasthan State pipeline should be laid by. the Gas Autho¬ 
rity of India Limited; 

And whereas it appears that for the purpose of laying such 
pipeline, it is necessary to acquire the right of user in the 
land described in the schedule annexed hereto; 

Now, therefore in exercise of the powers conferred by sub¬ 
section (1) of the Section 3 of the Petroleum and Mincials 
Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in the Land) Act, 
1962 (50 of 19621, the Cetural Government hereby declares 
Its intention to acquire the right of user therein : 

Provided that any person interested in the said land may, 
within 21 days from the date of this notificaticm, object to 
the laying of the pipeline under the land to the Competent 
Authority, Oil & Natural Gas Commission, Construction A 
Maintenance Division, H. B, J. Gas Pipeline Project, 49, 
Indra Colony. SaWai Madhopur; 

And every person making such an obieclion shall also state 
specifically whether he wishes to he heard in person or by 
legal practitioner.

S.O. 985.—^Whereas it appears to the Central Government 
that it is necessary in the public interest that for the trans¬ 
port of Petroleum from Hajra—Bareily to lagdishpur in 
Uttar Pradesh State Pipeline should be laid by the Gas 
Authority of India Limited; 

And whereas it appears that for the purpose of laying such, 

e inc, it is necessary to acquire the right of user in the 
described in the schedule annexed hereto; 

Now, therefore, it exercise of the powers conferred by 
sub-section (1) of the Section 3 of the Petroleum and Mine¬ 
rals Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in the Land) 
Act, 1962 (50 of 1962), the Central Government hereby de¬ 
clares its intention to acquire the right of user therein; 

Provided that any person interested in the said land may, 
within 21 days from the date of this notification, object to 
the laying of the pipeline under the land to the Competent 
Authority. Oil and Natural Gas Commission, H.B.J. Pipeline 
Project B-58/B, Aliganj, Lucltnow-226020, U.P. 

And every person making such an objection shall also state 
specifically whether he wishes to be heard in person or by 
legal practitioner.

S.O. 995.—Whereas it appears to the Central Government 
that it is necessary in the public interest that for the trans¬ 
port of Petroleum from Hajra-Burcily to Jagdishpur in Uttar 
Pradesh State Pipeline should be laid by the Gas Authority 
of India Limited; 

And whereas it appears that for the ptirpose of laying such 
pipeline, h is necessary to acquire the right of user in the 
land described in the schedule annexed hereto; 

Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub¬ 
section (1) of the Section 3 of the Petroleum and Minerals 
Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in the Land) Act, 
1962 150 of 1962), the Central Government hereby declares 
its intention to acquire the right of user therein; 

Provided that any person interested in the said land may, 
within 21 days from the date of this notification, object to the 
laying of the pipeline under the land to the Competent 
Authority Oil & Natural Gas Commission. H. B. J, Pipeline 
Project 8-58/8, AliganJ Luckno\v-226020 U.P. 

And every person making such an objection shall also state 
specifically whether he wishes to bo heard In person or by 
legal practitioner.

S.O. loll. —Whereas it appears to the Central Government 
that h is necessary in the public interest that for the transport 
of Petroleum from Hajira—Bareilly tojagdlsbpur i Uttar 
Pradesh State Pipeline should be laid by the Gas Authority 
of India Limited; 

And whereaa it appears that for the purpose of layinc such 
pipeline, it Is necessary to acquire the right of user in the 
land described in the schedule annexed hereto; 

Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub¬ 
section (1) of the Section 3 of the Petroleum and Minerals 
Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in the Land) Act, 
1962 (SO of ^62), the Central Government hereby declares 
its intention to acquire the right of user therein; 

Provided that any person interested in the said land may, 
within 21 days from the date of this notification object to 
the laying of the pipeline under the land to the Competent 
Authority Gas Authority, of India Ltd., H.B.J. Pipeline 
Project B-58/B, Allganj, Lucknow-226020, U.p, 

And every person making such an objection shall also state 
speclfloally whether he wishes to bo heard In person or by 
legal practtlioner.

MINISTRY OF STEEL, MINES AND COAL 
(Department of Coal) 

New Delhi, the 19th February, 1985 

S.O. 1022 :—Whereas It appears to the Central Government that coal is likely to bo obtained from the lands mentioned 
in the Schedule hereto annexed; 

Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) of section 4 o f the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Dev- 
lopment) Act, 1957 (20 of 1957), the Central Government hereby gives notice of its intentic n to prospect for coal therein; 

ThePlanNo.Rcv/02/84dated the 4th June, 1984 of the area covered by this notification can be inspected at the OflSce of the 
Central Coalfields Limited, (Revenue Section), Darbhanga House, Ranchi, or at the Office of the Deputy Commissioner, Giridih Bihar) 
or at the Office of the Coal Controller, 1, Council House Street, Calcutta; 

All persons interested in the land covered by this notification shall deliver all maps, charts and other documents referred to in sub 
section (7) of section 13 of the said Act to the Revenue Officer, Central Coalfields Limited, Darbhanga House, Ranchi within 90 days 
from the date of the publication of this notification In the Official Gazette.

S.O. 1047.—Whereas Messrs Godrei & Boyce Maaufac- 
turins Company Private Cimited, Pirojsha Nagar, Vikhroli, 
Bombay-40C079 (Mil, 26) (hereinafter referred to as the 
said establishnent) hav; appU?d for exemption tinder sub¬ 
section (2A) of section 17 of the Employees’ Provident Funds 
and Miscella^ieous Provisions Act, 1952 (19 of 1952) (here¬ 
inafter referred to as the said Act). 

And whereas, the Cential Government i& satisfied that the 
employees of the said establishment are, without making 
any separate contribution or payment of premium, in en¬ 
joyment, of benefits under the Group Insurance Scheme of 
the Life Insurance Scheme of the Life Insurance Corpora¬ 
tion of India in the nature of life insurance which are more 
favourable to such employees than the benefits admissible 
under the Employees’ Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme, 1976 
(hereinafter referred to as the said Scheme); 

Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub¬ 
section (2A) of section 17 of the said Act and in continua¬ 
tion of the notification of the Government of India in tha 
Ministry of Labour S.O. 909 dated the Rth February, 1982 
and subject to the conditions specified in the Schedule annexed 
hereto the Central Government hereby exempts the said 
establishment from the operation of all the provisions of the 
said Scheme for a further period of' three years with effect 
frori 27th t^’.-bruary, 1985 npto and inclusive of the 2,6th 
February, 1988. 

SCHEDULE 

1. The employer in relation to the said establishment shall 
submit such returns to 'he Regional Provident Fund Com¬ 
missioner. Maharashtra and malnlain such accounts and provide 
sueh faciltics for insnectign as the Central Govemment may 
direct from time to time. 

2. The employer shall pay such Inspection charges as the 
Central Govemment may, from time to time, direct under 
clause (a) of sUb-sretion (3A) of section 17 of the said Act 
within 15 days from the clo^e of every month 

3. All expenses involved in the administration of the Group 
Insurance ^herne including mainfainancs of accounts, sub¬ 
mission of returns, payment of insurance premia, transfer of 
accounts, payment of inspection charges etc. shall be home 
by the employer. 

4. The employer shall display on the Notice Board of the 
establishments, a copy of the rules of the Group Insurance 
Scheme as approved by the Central Government and, as and 
when amended , alongwith a translation.of the salient features 
thereof, in the language of the majority of the employees. 

5. Whereas an employee, who is already a member of the 
Employees’ Provident Fund or the Provident Fund of an 
establishment exempted under the said Act, is employed in 
his establishment, the employer shall Immediately enrol him 
as a member of the Group Insurance Scheme and pay neces¬ 
sary premium in respect of him to the Life Insurance Corpora¬ 
tion of India. 

6. The employer shall arran.go to enhance the benefits 
available to the employees under the Group Insurance Scheme 
appropriately, if the benefits' vailablo to the employees under 
the said Scheme are enhanced so that the benefits available 
under the Group Insurance Scheme arc more favourable to 
the employees than the benefits admissible tinder the .said 
Scheme. 

7. Notwithstanding anythinK contained in the Group In¬ 
surance Scheme, if on the death of an employee the amount 
payable undftr this scheme be less than the amount that 
would be payable had employee been covered under the said 
Scheme, the cmnlover shall pay the, difference to the legal 
heir/nominee of the employe® as compensation. 

8. N6 amendment of the'provisoins of the Group Insurance 
SchcTtle, shall be made without the prior approval of the Re- 
v’onel Prpvir'rnt Fund Commls'”’oner, Mahsrashira and where 
any amendment Is llkelv to affect adversely the interest of 
the einniovees, the Recional provident Commissioner shall 
heforS'' glvthg his'approval, give a reasonble opportunitv to 
the employees to explain their point of view. 


9. Whore, for any reason, the employees of the said estab¬ 
lishment do not remain covered under the Group Insurance 
Scheme of the Life Insurance Corporation of India as already 
adopted by the said establishment, or the benefits to ttic em¬ 
ployees under this Scheme are reduced in any manner, the 
exemption shall be liable to be cancelled. 

10. Where, for any reason, the employer fails to pay the 
premium; etc. within the due date, as fixed by the Life hi- 
SETance Corporation of India, and the policy is allowed to 
laps®, the exemption is liable to be cancelled. 

11. In case of default, if any made by the employer in 
payment of premium the responsibility for payment assu¬ 
rance benefits to the nominees or the legal heirs of deceased 
members who would have been covered under the said Scheme 
but for grant of this exemption, shall be that of the employer. 

12. Upon the death of the members covered under the 
Scheme the Life Insurance Corporation of India shall prompt, 
payment of the sum assured to the nominee or the legal heirs 
of the deceased member entitled for it and in any case within 
one month from the receipt of claim complete in aU respects.

AWARD 

The Government of India, Ministry of Labour by its 
Order No. L-3401(2)/82-DIV (A) dated July. 1982 refer¬ 
red the following dispute under Sections 7A and l(Xl)(d) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 between the Manage¬ 
ment of Visakhapatnam port Trust and their workmen, to 
this Tribunal for adjudication ; 

“Whether the action of the management of Visakha¬ 
patnam Port Trust in denying the benefit of two 
increments to the Operator of the Ore Handling 
Complex who were promoled from Grade III to 
Grade II during the period from 1-1-74 to 14-7-77 
vis-a-vis the prov'sions of Clause 2(m) of the settle¬ 
ment dated 14-7-77 with the Federations is iusti- 
fied ? If not, to what relief are the concerned 
workmen entitled ?" 

This reference was registered as Industrial Dispute No, 28 of 
1982 and noticed were issued to both the parties. 

2. The workmen filed their claim statement .stating that 
the dispute related to fixation of scales of pay in respect of 
Operators Grade HI and Grade II of Ore Handling Com¬ 
plex. According to them, originally there were two separate 
scales for Grade II and Grade Ill Operator.s and Grade 111 
Operators who were in the scale of Rs. 170—-290 while Grade 
II Operators were the scale of Rs. 150—253. The Wage 
Revision Committee recommended many other things a 
common scale for both the Grades in the scale of Rs. 450— 
700 and they were asked to be des'gnatcd as Grade II One- 
rators. Tt is ment'oned that a settlement was arrived at on 
14-7-1977 and the Revised Wace ScaT was to be imple¬ 
mented with effect from 1-1-1974, Clause 2(m) of the 
Settlement reads as follows :— 

“Merely as a consequence of lmplcmen*at'on of the 
recommendations of the Wage Revision Committee 
any facilhy, privilege, aminity, benefit, monetary 
or otherwise or concession tij which an employee, 
might he entitled by way of practice or usage 
shall not be withdrawn reduced or curtailed except 
to the extent and manner as pro'idod for in tb’s 
agreement.”

‘■‘Whether the action of the management of Citi Bank 
N. A New Delhi in calling upon the tellers em¬ 
ployed in their Branch at Parliament Street, New 
Delhi to visit the premises of their customers to 
collect cash and cheques from them is justified ? If 
not, to what relief are tbe workmen concerned 
entitled?” ■ 

2. The management of the Citi Bank requested the tellers 
employed in the branch at Parliament Street to visit the 
premises of their customers namely Saudi Arabian Airlines 
to collect cashichfeues. The workmen,felt that this was not 
job of Teller in the cash department and it involved them 
in unnecessary r sk and was ue-w duty imposed on them and 
was against the provisions of Bank Awards and Settlements 
under which the deposkers/customers had 'to present them¬ 
selves at the business premises, of the bank itself for making 
deposits of cash/cheques etc. This new practice was said to 
have been started since February,78 contrary to Bank rules 
and regulations. 

3. The Management contested the claim and asserted that 
th s was a normal banking service and carrying cash instru¬ 
ment is onp of the legitimate duties which the management 
can ask the member of the staff to perform and there is noth¬ 
ing foreign to the duties performed by the persons concerned 
in carrying cash or instruments. 

4. In view of tbe fact that at the time of reference 'was 
made there was only one party to which the workmen were 
sent for collecting cashicheques but later more such parties, 
have been added but the evidence relates only to the period 
before tbe reference made in 1980. 

5. The workmen felt that a better case could be set up to 
challenge the new practice by being able to show that the 
matter was not occasional or unique but was becoming a 
regular one, and it was felt that a new dispute may be raised 
with the management on the subsequent facts after adding the 
subsequent facts after 1978 and for that reason they requested 
that the dispute may, be deemed withdrawn and they would 
raise a new dispute in view of the practice becoming common 
and not remaining single or unique in relation to Saudi 
Arabian Airlines. 

6. Under the circumstances aforesaid a ‘No Dispute’ 
Award is made in respect of tbe dispute referred for adjudi¬ 
cation in this Tribunal.

AWARt) 

The Central Government, Ministry of Labour vide order 
No. L-I2012|254|82-D. IV(A) dated 25th August 1983, 
made the reference of the following dispute to this tribunal 
for Adjudication:— 

“Whether the action of the management of Banaras 
State Bank in relation to their Agra Branch is not 
absorbing Shri Rishi Muni temporary peon in the 
Bank’s services and terminating his services with 
effect from 20-7-82 is justified? If not,-to what 
relief is the workman concerned is entitled". 

1. The workman was appointed as peon with effect from 
1st December, 1981 against the regular permanent vacancy 
and was allowed to work till 6-2-82, On 7-2-82 when the 
workmen reached the bank he was not allowed to work and 
the Branch Manager appointed some other man. The work¬ 
man made a written representation on 13-2-82 which the 
Branch Manager with his recommendation forwarded to the 
Bank’s Head Office, The Bank reinstated the workman on 
12-6-82 and ho was allowed to work till 2f)th July, 1982 
with) some artificial Irreaks, The Branch Manager again 
terminated the services of the workman without any notice 
or written order on 20lh July, 1982 and paid salary only 
upto 17th July, 1982, After terminating the workman the 
Branch Manager appointed new band at his place. Thus 
the action of the Management’s arbitrary, malafide illegal 
and amounts to unfair labour practice and should be qua.shcd 
by this Hon’ble court on that account, It is further prayed 
that the workman bo deemed to bo in the regular employ¬ 
ment of the bank with full back wages and other bene¬ 
fits. 

2. The cose of the Management Bank is that workman 
Rishi Muni was employed from time to time only to meet 
the exigencies of tl^ requirements as temporary peon and 
it would he incorrect to say that he was appointed against 
the regular and permanent vacancy, hence his absorption in 
the banks senn'ce can not be claimed as a matter of right 
which is only prerogative function of the management. The 
management admits that in span December, 1981 to July, 
1982 the workman worked only for 89 days with 4 tem¬ 
porary breaks. 

3. In the rejoinder filed by the workman ho has asserted 
that in fact he was appointed against regular permanent 
vacancy created due to transfer of a permanent peon else¬ 
where. 

4. The proceedings initially started in the Industrial Tri¬ 
bunal Delhi, which was transferred to newly created CGIT 
Kanpur. On the first date in thie Kanpur Tribunal one 
Shri N. K. Bhargawa, appeared for the Management. There¬ 
after on all subsequent dates none appeared for the Manage¬ 
ment. It was the duty of the management to have found 
out as to what dates have fixed for after the first hearing on 
transfer at Kanpur. However, by way of abandon caution 
registered notice was issued to the management twice but 
none appeared, hence the case was ordered to proceed 
eXparfe against tlw Management. Workman filed alfidavlt 
in support of his contention and verified the same before the 
court. 

5. In his aiiidavit he ascerted that he was appointed against 
the regular and permanent vacancy on 1st December. 1981 
and continuously worked till 6th Februarv, 1982 He was 
not allowed to work on 7tb February, 1982 and one Mabesb 
Kumar Shyama was apnointed in bis nlacp on which he 
made representation in writing which he has filed and is 
.Annexure ‘A on the record. It was on this representation 


(hat he was reinstated with effect from I2-6-I982 and 
allov.'ed to work till 2(Jth July, 1982. His services were 
terminated without any notice and without, any written order 
on said 20th July, 1982, The Branch Manager again ap¬ 
pointed some new hands namely Gurbachan Singh, Bankey 
Bchari, Suresh Goe), etc.. He again representated to the 
Management but when he failed Ije raised Industrial Dis¬ 
pute. 

6. It is common ground that neither appointment letter 
was Issued nor any termination order was given further there 
is no denial on oath of the fact that the workman was 
appointed on a permanent nature of job in the vacancy 
created by transfer of one of the workman of the branch. 
The Management has failed to show that he was appointed 
for a limited period for work which was essentially of a 
temporary nature or employed temporarily as an additional 
workman in connection with the temporary increase in work 
of a permanent nature. It is also not the case of the 
management that he was appointed temporarily in the ab¬ 
sence of a particular permanent workman. The Manage¬ 
ment had been creating temporary breaks so that the work¬ 
man may not acquhe any legal rights which is evident 
from the report of tht bank appended to the application of 
the workman filed as Annexure ‘A’ in which it is specifically 
written that if the workman is re-employed he will not he 
allowed to complete 240 days In a year. Further if the 
work was there and after his termination It was necessary 
to appoint another man he should have been given a chance 
and compliance of provision of section 25 G and H should 
have been complied with, The Management should have 
maintained a register of such temporary workers and applied 
the principles of last come first go. As the management 
did not observed anv of tljese provisions of the l.D. Act 
nor provisions of Bi-partite nor of Shasfri's Award, The 
termination of the services of the workman after taking 
work from him for 89 days was illegal unjust and malafide 
and temporary breaks were shown with thft malafide in¬ 
tention so that he may not acquire the status of the per¬ 
manent employee. I accordingly believing the affidavit of 
the workman hold (hat the action of the Management of 
the Betiaras State Bank Limited in relation to their Agra 
Branch in not absorbing Shri Rishi Muni Temporary Peon 
in the Bank’s services and terminating his seiwices with effect 
frorn 20-7-1982 is not justified. The result is that he is 
entitled to be re-instated wilh full back wages and continui¬ 
ty of service and all benefits. 

7. I, therefore, give my award accordingly.

2. The dispute is : 

“Whether the action oil the management of South Malabar

relief is (he vrorkman concerned entitled 

3. On receipt of notice issued by this Tribunal, tlie paities 
appeared. 

I 

4. The Petitioner filed the claim statement raising the 
following grounds to sustain his case . The Petitioner 
joined the services of (he Respondent-Bank as a junior clerk 
with effect from 10-111-1979. The Petitioner applied for 
leave from 1-2-1982 to 6-2-1982 and the same was sanctioned 
by the Respondent. The Petitioner as he fell ill sent a 
leave letter supported by a medical certificate through his 
brother Vinod Kumar on 8-2-1982 and the same was handed 
over to the Branch Manager. Tlic leave was for a reriod 
of 30 days. The Respondent did not send any lepiy. The 
Petitioner had to leave for Deffii as his sister was very seriously 
ill. His brother-in-law met with an accident at Dubai and 
he had to rush to that country in March, 1982. The Peti¬ 
tioner’s hrother-in-law succumbed lo ids injuries and the 
petitioner had to stay b.ack. Alt thes,j developments were 
intimated to the Braitch Manager orally by the relatives of 
the Petitioner. 

5. The Petitioner when he returned to Calicut he received 
the order dated 12-4-1982 of the Respondent terminating his 
services with effect from 8-2-1932 on the grormd of abandon¬ 
ing his employment. The Petitioner protested against the 
illegal termination and requested the Respondent to reinstate 
him in service. The older dated 12-4-1982 terminating the 
services of the Petitioner is illegal. 


6. The South Malabar Grarnn Bank (Staff) Service Re¬ 
gulations, 1980 will apply toi the Petitioner. The Respon¬ 
dent have not followed the provisions of these regulations. 
The termination is arbitrary and iliegal. The Respondent' 
have not complied with ttie conditions prescribed under 
Regulation 10(2). The Respondent have no powers to ter¬ 
minate the services of any employee automatically on the 
alleged ground of abandonment. The Respondent ought to 
have taKen disciplinary action against the Petitioner as 
contemplated under Regufation 22(2). The Respondent 
laded to follow the procedure laid down under Regulation 
30(2). The Respondent have not provided any opportunity 
to the Petitioner to prodv>ce satistactory explanation regarding 
his leave. The impugned order of termination is violative 
of the principles of natural justice. The Respondent has 
failed to comply with the maudaiory conditions prescribed 
under Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act. This 
Hon’blc Tribunal may be pleased to pass an award setting 
aside the order of termination dated 12-4-1982 and direct 
the reinstatement of the Petitioner with continuation of 
service and ail other attendant benefits, award costs and 
render justice. 

7. The Management filed counter statement resisting the 
claim of the Petitioner on the follov/ing grounds ; The Peti¬ 
tioner should have ioined diiiy on 8-2-1982. He did not do 
so nor did he make any application for leave. On 19-3-1982 
a medical certificate was delivered through a messenger need¬ 
ing absence from duty for 30 days from 8-2-1982. Since 
there was no leave application, the medical certificate was 
not taken cognizance of. The Petitioner had left India. 
On 23-3-1982, a letter was sent to the Petitioner pointing out 
his absence without leave from 8-2-1982, granting him time 
till 31-3-1982 to report tor work cautioning him that if he 
failed to report for duty on or before 31-3-1982 his name 
would be removed, i'he Petitioner did not report for 
work by 31-3-1982. The Respondent treated the Petitioner 
as having abandoned his job with eft'ect from 8-2-1982. The 
Petitioner even collected his earned wages and addressed a 
letter dated 17-7-1982 for payment of bonus dues. The 
bonus was also paid to him. Subsequent to April, 3982, 
the Petitioner accepted his non-employment and corresponded 
with the Management lor payment of his dues with no inten¬ 
tion of resuming his iob. The cessation of employment of 
the Petitioner was brought about by reason of his continuous 
absence and it was by way of abandonment of job. There 
was no termination of employment by the Respondent. It 
was the Petitioner who terminated the employment. 

8. It is denied that the Petitioner sent leave letter for 
his absence after 6-3-1982. Unless the leave Ts granted one 
cannot presume that leave has been sanctioned. At no time 
prior to 31-10-1982, the Petitioner protested against the 
cessation of his employment. The order dated 12-4-1982 
is not really an order of terminition. It is a case of aban¬ 
donment of job and the reference to termination of serveie 
and superfluous. Since the cessation of employment of the 
Petitioner was brought about by his own conduct, there was 
no question of applying the provisions of service regulations. 
The Petitioner had accepted the cessation of employment. 
The Petitioner did not respond to the Mana.uement's Icltcr 
dated 23-3-1982, directing the Petitioner to lei'oit for work 
on Or before 31-3-1982. There was no option left to the 
Bank than to treat him as having abandoned his employ¬ 
ment. As he had already abandoned his job, there was a 
termination of his employment. Since there was no leave 
letter, the Management Bank was not obliged to consider 
the medical certificate. This Honourable Court may be 
pleased to make an award i ejecting the claim of the Petitioner. 

9. M. Ws .1 and 2 and W.W.l were examined. Exs. M-1 
to M-2l were marked. 1 have heard the learned counsel for 
the Petitioner and the learned counsel for the Management. 

10. The point for consideration is whether the termina¬ 
tion of the services of the Petitioner Sri E. Vijayarajan 
ftom 8-2-1982 is justified. 

11. The agreement between the Respondent-Bank and the 
Petitioner-Employee at the time of initial appointment is 
Ex. M-1. The most r=;levant terms in this agreement Ex. 
M-1 will be only Terms 17, 18 and 19. Under these terms 
the employee is .entitled to the leave that may be available 
to' his under the provisions of the Service Code. He shall

the; gazette of India : march 9, I985/PHALGUNA is, 1906 [Part 11— Stc. 3 (ii)J 


be liable to disciplinary action in respect of any misconduct 
On his part and the employee may retire or be required 
to retire, or may resign or may leave the services or the 
Bank or have his services terminated in accordance with 
the provisions of the Service Code. Therefore the vitrious 
modes by which the services of the employee can come to 
an end are indicated in term 19 of the agreement Ex. M-1. 
But that in turn should be in accordance with the provisions 
Of the Service Code. The Service Cotie of this Respondent- 
Bank is marked as Ex. M-12. It is captioned as South 
Malabar Grarrin Bank (Stall) Service Regulations, 1980. 
The regulations which are relevant for consideration in 
this case will be 10, 22 and 30. Before dealing with the 
real' meaning and the applicability of the above mentioned 
regulations it becomes necessjiy to go into the facts and 
the evidence in this case. 

12. It is not disputed that initially this Petitioner applied 
for leave from 1-2-1982 to 6-2-'982 and the leave was sanc¬ 
tioned. 7-21982 happened to be heiday and therefore the 
employee was bound lo report for duty on 8-2-1982. How¬ 
ever, on 8-2-1982, the employee did not lepoit for duty. 
But instead he sent a medic.sl ceitificate through his brother.

t leave application in the prescribed form the Branch Manager

Later, he sent that medical ceitificate to the Head Office

the Head Office, under which he has indicated that the

I’eave application has been submitted oy the employee. The 
Head Office has written a letter Ex. M-I4 according to the

M-14 that the employee had been absent from duty without

and his name will be removed from the rolls. According to 
the evidence of the employee, there is an application pres¬ 
cribed for applying for leave. He submitted the medical 
certificate Ex. M-3 with his letter through his brother and 
later due to unavoidable and compel ling circumstances he 
had to go to Delhi where his sister was ill and later he had 
to go to Dubai where his brother-iii-iaw met with an accident 
and ultimately died. After coming back to the place where 
was. working in the Bank he approached the Bank and orally 
asked for reinstatement. These are the facts and evidence. 
The Bank had issued Ike order Ex. M-18 dated 12-4-1982, 
in which the Bank has narrated the absence of the employee 
from duty without permission of ^he authority and the 

failure of the employee to report for duty on or before 
31-3-1982 pursuant to the letter Ex. M-14 atijl under the 
circumstances, the Bank was conipelled to terminate the 
services of the eirsployce with effect from 8-2-1982. Of 

course, the Bank has indicated that it was on account of 

abandonment of job by him. 

13. .It is true the employee dcoied. Ihc receipt of the 

letter Ex. M-14. This is proved to be false by the docu¬ 
ments. Ex. M-14 is dated 23-3-1982. In Ex. M-8, dated 
31-10-1982, a fetter written by the employee to the Bank, 
there is an express reference to the letter of the Bank 
dated 23-3-1982. That letter dated 23-3-1982 should only 
refer to Ex. M-14. It is, in that letter the employee’s absence 
from duty without feave or permission had been mentioned 
and he had been directed lo repon. for duty on or before 
31-3-1982 and it has also been noied that if he tailed to 
report for duty he v/ill be deemed to have abandoned the 
service and his name will be lemoved. Therefore the claim 
of the employee that he did not receive the ktler Ex M-l4 
is falsified by his own letter Ex. M-S. 

14. Accepting all the above facts and the evidence it be¬ 
comes necessary to examine whether the employee has aban¬ 
doned and thereby brought about <-i cessation of service. 
Even if it is so, an ancillary aspect v/ill be whether such a 
situation wilf be in accordance with tbe Service Re.gvlations 
Ex. M-12. As has 'oeen already indiciijed Regulation 1l> 
contemplates termination of service by issue of notice and 
the notice must be in writting addressee to the Chairiwin of 
the Bank and it is one month’s notice. Under sub-clause 


(2) of the Regulation 10, the Bank inav terminate the service 
of an employee by giving one tr«nth’s notice or pay in lieu 
thereof. None of these things had been done, either by the 
employee or by the Bank. Jn spite of my very careful read¬ 
ing of the various regulations in Ex. M-12, I do not find any 
regulation under winch the services of an employee can be 
brought to an end by voluntary abandonment of the j'ob. In 
fact, M.'W.2 in his evidence admitted that they treated the 
Petitioner as having abandoned his job and recorded it 
accordingiy. But he cannot refer to any regulation under 
which the abandonment of the job by the employee was 
recorded. Therefore, as per the terms of th-e agieement bet¬ 
ween the parlies Ex. M-l, the services of employee can be 
terminated only in accordance with the provisions of the 
Service Code. But the Service Regulations Ex. M-12 do 
not Contemplate tne termination of the services of the 
employee by the employer for abandoning the job. It is 
pertinent to point out that Ex. M-4, dated 12-4-1982 uses 
the terminology that the services of the employee aie tei- 
minated wdth effect from 8-2-1982 Inter alia it refers to 
the letter of the Bank dated 23-3-1982 which is Ex. M-14. 
Ex. M-14 i sdated 23-3-1982 ana it gives a direction to the

18. When the services of the employee are governed by the

and invalid.

ISSUES FINDINGS 

1. Whether the enquiry held by the 

Enquiry Officer was fair and 

proper ? Yes 

2. Whether the findinjts noted by him 

were just, proper or perverse? Just and proper. 

Not perverse. 

3. Whether the punishment awarded was

4. To what relief or reliefs, if any, 

the workman is entitled ? As per order. 

5. What order ? As per Order. 

REASONS 

6. It is contended on behalf of the workman that the 
charge as it stands is vague in the sense that it does not 
refer to any misconduct stipulated in para 19.5 of the First 
Bipartite Settlement which binds both the parties and there¬ 
for© if the very charge which is the foundation of the enquiry 
falls, the resultant enquiry also must give way. Before the 
chargesheet it seems a notice was Issued to the workman as 
seen from; Ex. B’-annexed to the statement of claim where 
the incident as is alleged to have occiired is narrated namely 
that one of the bundles ivhich were entrusted to the work¬ 
man for stitching when examined was found to be minus 
seven currency notes of Rs. 100 denomination. This vvas 
followed by chargesheet Ex, D dated 17-5-1978 which also is 
nothing but the repetition of the notice. While examining 
the charces we cannot forget one thing that it was not issued 
by a judicial authority and therefore the test laid down for 
judicial action would he of no avail for determining tlie 
validity or othei’wise of the same. Wh.at is expected is whether 
the charge.s aives the complete idea to the workman who is 
to face it about the alienation levelled against him which 
allegation the management ultimately is expected to estab¬ 
lish so that if neoessary the workman has an opportunity 
to meet the same. It is not therefore the form, it is not 
therefore the letter but the spirit and substance which is to 
govern the legality and propriety of the charge and when 
viewed accordingly the conteniiou that while stitching the 
notes there was a shortage of seven currency notes of 
Rs. 100 and that- It was (he workman who was instrumen¬ 
tal in removing the same, finds in the charge in no way the 
same can be said to he vague on the contrary specific 
details are to be noticed. 

7. To strike at the root of the whole thin it was tried 
to be urged that the facts as indicated do not fall within 
the four comers of the misconduct as described 
in para. 19.5 of the First Bipartite Settlement and if the 
act do,es not amouhl to misconduct there cannot be any 
order of discharge or ,my ord.'v of punishment much less 
the order of discharc. As the facts stand the allegation is 
that the workman removed seven currency notes of Rs. 100 
denimination from the bundles which was entrusted to him 
lor stitching. It was therefore an allegation of loss of Bank 
property caused wilfully by the workman and therefore if 
we peruse para. 19.5 at clause fd) we do come across the 
misconduct described as wilful demage or attempt to cause 
damage to the property of the Bank or any of its customers. 
The property may include movable and immovable and there¬ 
fore when the allegation is that there was a theft of Rs. 700 



1284 


IPart TI— Sue. 3 (iij]

torninitted by the Peon, the nllogation was of wilful clainapc 
to the property of the Bank and as such the contention that 
the act even if established cannot constitute a misconduct as 
contemplated by the First Bipartite Settlement can carry 
no force. 

8. During the enquiry when it commenced the record 
shovys that a request was made by the workman to appoint 
Sto D. V. Yardi, as his Advocate, otherwise all,east allow 
him to be represented by Shri R. D. Jog, Leader of the

to the plea that having regard to the gravity of the charge 
if the defence was required to be conducted by the workman 
himself without any aid there is violatio^j of the principlc.s 
of natural justice. If at all the discretion which vested with 
the management, it is urged, was to h; exercised it should 
have been exercised in favour of the workman and defence 
nid if not by an Advocate at least of Shri Jog should have 
been provided for. In this connection the Bipartite Settlement 
clause 19.12 reads that an employee shall he permitted to 
be defended by a representative of a registered Bade union 
of bank employees of which he is a member, where the 
employee is not a member Of any trade union of bank em¬ 
ployees. by a representative of the registered trade union of 
the Bank in which he is employed or with the Bank’s pei mis¬ 
sion by a lawyer or at the request of the Union by a represen¬ 
tative of the state federation or all India Organisation to 
which such union is, affiliated. Neither there is request by 
union nor Shri R. D. log falls iu anv of the category and 
therefore this leaves us with the question of appointn'cnt of 
an Advocate. The Bipartite Settlement which is binding, as 
already stated, on both the parties contemplates appointment 
of a Lawyer but that must be with the Bank’s permission. 
What is contended i.s that if at all there is a discretion they 
should have used in favour of the workman for appointment 
of an Advocate but in rny view when the parties have en¬ 
tered into a settlement and when the Bank’s permission is 
a condition precedent, mere refusal of such permission cannot 
invalidate the action of the Bank. Certainly in recent case 
namely in the case between the Board of Trust.ees of Port 
of Bombay Vs. Dilipkumar K- Nadkarni reported in 1983 (I) 
LLJ, page 1 their Lordship of the Supreme Court, held when 
it was found that the employers’ representative was duly 
qualified, it was incumbent on the management to permit the 
workman also to bo defended by an Advocate. One fact 
however, is to he borne in mind that the rules of the Port 
Trust were silent and did not inhibit the defence by a legal

14. In a proceeding i.ndcr Section HA of the Industrial 
Disputes Act the management cannot plead iliai absolute 
rigtu is vested wiUi them to uwind punishment blit it is .subjects 
to judicial scrutiny and tlicrelore it n is lounj that ihe 
punishment is disproportionate, then it may be lowered 
down. Ill this connection ii is iiue that die employee is 
found to be removing notes from the bundles entrusted to 
him, yet it is an admitted case that within a short time the 
money was restored to the Bank; and no loss was sulftred by 
anybody in the matter. Hven then the act has to be taken 
serious note of but this docs not mean that the employes 
must be sent home for tJic said purpose. Here is a young 
man who had joined the service some two years baok, be¬ 
longing to the poor strata of society, record shows that his 
father was a Municipal Driver whilo- the mother is a nurse. 
If therefore such a person due to temptation or otherwise 
acted in a foolish manner, .some credit will have to he given 
to the immediate restoration of the currency notes and the 
writing dated 31-1-1978 expre.ssing regret and guaranteeing 
good conduct. What punishment should be awarded would 
depend upon the facts of each case. My attention was drawn 
to the Bombay High Court judgement where mere refusal by 
a Stenographer to obey Ihc order of the superior I'd 
the order of dismissal and the High Court put the seal upon 
it. In the (Jasc Ved Prakash Gupta V.s. M/s. Delion Cable 
India (P) Ltd, reported in (1984) 2 SSC page 560 their 
Lordships of the Supreme Court held that the use of abu,«ive 
language against co-worker should not result in dismissal. 
In another case between Bhagut Ram Vs. State of Himachal 
Pradesh reported in (1983) 2 SSc page 44B their Lordship 
of the Supereme Court held, that when no loss was caused 
the order of dismissal deserves to lx set aside. In the case 
between Gujarat State Road Transport Corporation, Ahmeda- 
bad Vs. Inmnadas Becharbhai reported in 1983 j.AB.l.C. 
page 1349 their Lordships of Gujarat High Court when the 
Bus Conductor was found pocketing the entire collection 
without issuing ticket observed that the Labour Court can 
depending upon facts and circumstances of the case and the 
offence, direct that he should bo absorbed in the workshop 
section or some other similar post which does not intolve 
daily handling of money. I have quoted these Instances which 
justifies my conclusion that what w'ould be a proper punish¬ 
ment would depend upon the facts of each case and there 
would he no yard-stick or universal rule for the same. In this 
connection without repeating the facts as stated above, upon 
the writing was obtained for the purpose of proof of theft, 
the latter part of such writing would have to be given due 
weight and therefore if the workman guaranteed good conduct, 
there is no reasihn for nbt giving that importance. F.vcn cri¬ 
minal jurisprudence recognises the probation of offenders end 
docs not like a culprit committing a siqnle misconduct be¬ 
coming, a hardened criminal Considering all these Hets, con¬ 
sidering no loss was caused, and having regard to the young 
age of the workman T am convinced that it is iiot the 
ortler of dismissal but sonlething lesser would be a proper 
order.

M. 'V, haralhi for the Petitioner relied upon the decision

a paiiiciilar puni.shment. Infact it is clearly laid down in

poinled out if the fact was brought to the notice of the 
employee he h.ad explained that he had no knowledge of 
the superior officer and he had adequate explanation to offer 
for the alleged remarks or that his conduct subsequent to 
the remarks had been exemplary • whether his explanation 
would he acceptable or not. The question to be seen was 
whether the employee is ,civen reasonable opportun'ty to 
give, explanation. The Court cannot accept the doctrinp of 
"presumptive knowledge" or that of “purposeless enquiry’’ 
as their acceptance will be subversive of the principles of 
reasonable opportunity. 1 respectively follow the said judge¬ 
ment and 1 fail to umjerstand that the Man.'igement did not 
bestow their attent'nn (n these principles of giving reasonable 
opponinity by serving these adverse notc.s Fx, M-1 and M-2 
on which Ex. M-3 was prepared to the Petitmner for being 
explained. Tn State of Orissa v DR (Miss) Biriarani Del 
(AIR 1967 S.C. page 1269) it was laid down thM the order 
of compulsory reiiroment based on certain disputed of date 
of b rth on the basis of the report of the Enquiry Officer who

voilatc the principles of natural Justice though It Is an admE

11. Moreover having regard to the relevant circumstances 
of the case I am of the strong opinion that the order of 
retirement applying Clause 18,1 of the Bi-partite settlement 
by the Management amounted to misuse of the provisions 
without any material indicating that the employees efficiency 
is impaired after reaching the age of 57 ycaiw as mentioned

(he Management that they have taken disciplinary action 
as contemplated under Chapter XIX of the Bi-partite settle¬

slowing down in performance of work or indecent behf,vioiir 
on the promises of the Bank or dis-ohedienco of any law¬

superiors as menlioncd therein. 

12. Thus the action of the Management of the State 
Bunk of Hyderabad, Hyderabad in relation to their Kanaka- 

iri Branch, District Raichur in terminating the services of 
ri P R. Pyati, Head Cashier by way of premature retire¬ 
ment with effect from 1-10-1977 is not justified and the 
Management is directed to calculate his pension .since he 
had already attained the age of 60 years (as the petitioner 
deposed that he is^aged 64 years at the date of deposition) 
with three years back wages of full salary' as well as the 
pensionary benefits including the moactarv beliefs appropriate 
to him by restriicfng his pension fixing the .age of retirement 
at 60 years should be calculated and the existing pension, if 
any, should be revised as per the usual established rules and 
practice of the Bank and paid to him.

AWARD 

Dated : jmiuary 31, 1983 

The Central Government in exercise of its powers under 
- Section 10 of the Indusrtial Disputes Act referred the follow¬ 
ing dispute vide Notification No, L. 12012(214)/82-D.lI(A) 
dated 28th June, 1983 ~ 

“Whether the action of the managmeent of the State 
Bank of India Region I, L.H.O. Bhopal, in termi¬ 
nating the services of Shri Ram Pyare, Sweeper 
with effect from 26-8-81 is justified ? If not, to what 
relief is the workman concerned entitled?’’ 

2. Rani Piyare had been serving in the Bhopal Main 
Branch of the State Bank of India (hereinafter called the 
Bank) between 15-8-1980 and 24-11-1980 as a part-time 
Sweeper in the Bank. He started v,/orldng in the Maharana 
Pratap Nagar Branch of the'Bank from 25-11-1980 and 
continued serving the Branch upto 25-8-1981 as a part-time 
Sweeper. In the Mahar.ina Pratap Nagar Branch, he did 
part time work for 219 days. 

3. The Bank has about 6000 branches in the country and 
is constituted under Ihe State Bank of India Act, 1955.* 
Each Branch is under the direct control and supervision of 
the Branch Manager who is answdfable to the Regional 
Office. The administrative work of each of the Branc'n is 
independent of the other. There are Regions and Zones for 
administrative purpose in the Bank which keep supervision 
and control respectively under the jur sdiction under them. 
The Branches inter se have no admiinstrative or supervisory 
control over the other. The Branch Manager is normally 
empowered to engage employees such as Messenger, Sweeper 
and such casual workers for a period not exceeding 90 days 
at a time. Ram Pyare was appointed on hourly basis, de¬ 
pending on the requirement, for two hours in a day to six 
hour* in a day. The part-time wor’sers could be appoint¬ 
ed by the Manager or anybody entrusted with the admini¬ 
stration of the Bank. For ali other r.ppointnifnts the re¬ 
cruitment was regulated by rules in this behalf. 

4. The workman claimed that he had' worked for more 
than 240 days in the State Bank of India and was accord¬ 
ingly entitled to he regularised. His employment could not 
be term'nated and such termination would be retrenchment 
w'hich in the present circumstances would be void as not 
in accordance with the provisions of Section 25-F of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. Therefore he claimed reinstatement 
with back wages. 

5. The Management of the Bank contends that Ram Payare 
was merely a part-time worker engaged to work on hcurly 
basis in the day. He could not he even called a casual worker. 
Moreover, he had not completed 240 dtiys of work within 
12 months at any time. Therefore the provisions of Section 
25F ibid would not be attracted. It is further ermtended that ■ 
the employment in one branch of the Bank of such a workman 
is not such as would count for total services in the Bank 
when employed in the other branch. The two branches aie 
separate establishments! and the service rendered in one 
branch would not enure him to his benfit in computing the 
240 days oFservices in 12 months while continuing service in 
another Branch. If he had worked in the Bhopal Main 
Branch, the neriod of service could he not added to service 
in another Branch for Ihe purpose of Section 25B of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. 

6 . There is no doubt that Ram Pyare workedi in the Bhopal 

Main Branch for 95 days as part-time worker i in the 

Maharana Pratap Nagar Branch as a nart-time r_ ir for 

219 davs on hourly basis. The Bank has hied a complete 
1 'st of the number of hours he worked on each day and from 
Ex. M/2 it is clear that sometimes he worked for two hours 
in the day to 6 hours in a day .and on cue occasion be 
worked for even 11 hours. He w'as paid according to the 

number of hours he ha-l worked. It is also interesting to 

note form the list of ,the working days of R-nm Pyare in 
both the offices that on about 11 days he had v/orked both 
ir, the Bhonal Main Branch and the Maharana Pratap Nagar 
Branch simultaneousiv. It appears ihat on these days, in 
♦hp morning he worked in the Maharana Pratap Nagar 
Branch and at other part of fh" dav in the Bhopal Main 
Branch. There are not fixed hours of work for a Sweeper. 


What he is required to do is to clean the premises before 
the business hours, theretore, it was possible to finish the 
work in the evening of the succeeding day and thus to 
manage working simitltancously at two different places. The 
main question is whether the working days in one branch 
in such part-time manner would be added to the number 
of days served by him in another Branch in a similar part- 
time manner for purpose of computing the length of service 
envisaged in Section 25B of the industrial Disputes Act. I 
am of the view that he cannot be given this benefit for the 
purpose of Section 25B of the Industrial Disputes Act. To 
begin with, he was a part-time worker and it. is difficult, 
to compute the number of working days of such a part- 
time employee. Section 25B of the Industrial Disputes Act 
envisages 240 days of actual .work within 12 months and 
w'hen this done it would hi deemed to be continuous emp¬ 
loyment for an year so -is to give the benefit contemplated 
in the chapter to the workm.an. An hour or two hours’ 
work in a day cannot be equated with a day’s work. It is 
also difficult to regularise such a person for he cannot be 
said to be regularised as a Sweepejr w'orking: two hours a day.- 
There are no permanent posts of part-time Sweepers in the 
Bank of the description where the number of working hours 
cuold vary in each day. This would be wholly incompatible 
with any systematic employment in a statutory body. 

7. It would be seen that Section 25B(ii)(a) of the Indus¬ 
trial Disputes Act envisages that the workman ought to 
have actually worked under the employer for not less than 
240 days. It is, .fiierefo.re, necessary ihat the worktruan 
must establish that lie had worked actually 240 days within 
12 months before the relevant date. A part-time worker 
of the nature in question cannot be said to have actually 
worked for a single day .'n the Bank. It is the days work 
that is contemplated. The worker in the instant case is not 
even a part-time worker of the Bank as the length of the 
hours^ of work was not fixed. He vas engaged each day 
to do the work for the number of hour, the employer want¬ 
ed him and his wages were cai’culated on the basis of hours. 
In his case it has already been shown that sometimes he 
worked for two hours a day and on another occasions he 
worked for more than two hours. In mv opinion. Section 
25B is not attracted for a workman of the category in 
question. 

8 . There is another difficultv in his case as! the workman 

cannot be said to be unler the same employer when he 
worked in two different branches. The recruitment m the 
Bank is governed by certain set of rules. Appointments of 
temporary nature are contemplated in paragraph 20.7 of the 
Sastri Award. Bi:l here he would not come in the cate¬ 
gory of the appointments contemplated by the Sastri Award. 
The power given to apop'ntment for such a worker was 
given to the Manager or the Office-in-Charge of the Branch., 
Therefore the workman was employed by one branch he 
cannot be said to be the servant of another branch. That 
being the case, in his case when he worked in Maharana 
Pratap Nagar Branch the establishment would not be. the 
State Bank of India as such, but the Maharana Bratap Nagar 
Branch of the State Bank of India. ‘Therefore he could not 
claim that the services renedered in Bhopal Ma’n Branch 
should be added to the Mabaratia Pratap Nagar Branch. 
The anomaly is clear that for 11 days he worked in both 
the Branches without the knowledge of the respective 
Managers. There is no irregul'arity in such cases being a 
part-time worker he could take up employment in any other 
estabilshment in his spare hours and LOid! ';'’.■ if l.e h: .1 
worked on the same d.ay in another !! . uh of ilie 
Bank of India he had worked under'a c‘.i:!b''>!!m(‘''i 

and not the same estabilshment for the purpose of Section 
25B of the Industrial Disputes Act. 

9. I am accordingly of the view that the workman has 
no claim to be regularised in anv of the Branches and his 
lermination with effect frotn 26-8-1981 was wholly justified. 

ORDFR.—In view of the reasons given above, the State 
Bank of India, Regions I. L.H.O. Bhopal, in. terminating 
the services of Shri Ram Pyare, Sweeper, with effect from 
26-8-1981 is justified. He is not. entitled to any relief. In 
the peculiar circumstances of the case there shall be no 
order as to 'costs. 

K. K. DUBE, Presiding Ofiicer

(12) Coming to (he decision referred to and relied on 
bv the. learned counsel appearing for the Union, after a very 
careful study of the decisions 1 opine that these decisionsi 
will not apply to the facts of this cave. The case reported 
in 1964—11, L.I..T. Page 633 (D. C. Dew an Mohideen 
Sahib & Sons and another vs. United Bidi Workers’ Union, 
Salem, tind another) is a ca.se, where on facts, the Supreme 
Court held that the employer had the right to direct what 
was to be done and also had the right to direct the 
manner in which it was to be tione. hi thtit ca.se. it was 
held that the so-called independ,ent contractors were mere 
agents or hianch manaseis of the pioprietor . Those inter¬ 
mediaries were found to be iinpeciuiioiis persons who could 
baldly atfoid to have their own factoiies. The contract in 
that case was held lo be praciicallv one-sided because the 
proprietor could at his choice supply the raw materials or 
refuse to do so and the «o-called contractors had no i (ght 
to insist upon the supply of raw materials to them. Tn that 
context, the real prnnrieior was considered to be the master 
or the very empfover. Therefore, ip mv view, the facts in 
that case are entirely difl'ereni and (hat authority will not 
heln the Union in this case. 

(13) 'The c'se repoilej in 1970-—If. T T-.T. Page 397 
(Hussainbhai. Calient vs. ,\Iaih Factory Thozilali IFnion. 




[»Tnr II— 3(ii)]

Calicut and others) also stands an entirely different facts. 
The employer in that case was found to have, economic con¬ 
trol over the workers’ sU'bsistence, skill and continued emp- 
ployment. The ptesence of intermediate contractors with 
whom alone the workers have immediate or direct rela¬ 
tionship ex contactu is of no consequence when, on lifting 
the veil or looking at the conspectus of factors, govering 
employment, the naked truth was d'seovered though drap- 
ped in different paper arrangement, that the real employer 
was the Management and not the immediate contractor. 

(14) In the case reported in 1983—IT, LU. Page 415 
(Shri Shambunath Goyal vs. Bank of Baroda and others) 
the Supreme Court found that the worker though he was 
paid at piece rate, he was under the control of the emp¬ 
loyer who had the r'ghi to reject the work .and who had 
the scope to refuse to give work and that particular aspect 
proved the existence of relationship of master and servant. 

1 am of the view that the facts in this decision are different 
and therefore that decision will not apply to the fact of 
this case. On that view of the matter, 1 have no hesitat on 
to reject the contention of the learned counsel appearing 
for the Union that this Petitioner-Deposit Collector Sri G. 
Selvaraj was a workman or employee of the Respondent- 
Bank. 

(15) It is also relevant to refer to an argument advanced 
by the learned counsel appearing for the Bank based upon 
Section 10 of the Banking Regulation Act. 1949. Seclion 10 
prohibits the Banking Company from employing any ‘peison 
whose remuneration or part of whose remuneration takes 
the form of Commission or Of a share in the pofils of the 
Company. But however, the Rank is permitted to appoint 
a person on payrront of commission under a contract other¬ 
wise than as a regular member of (he staff of the Company. 
TWs Section suggests that the Deposit Collector w’bo is 
only paid commission on the basis of the collections made 
by him and remitted into the Bank cannot become a mem¬ 
ber of the staff of the Company at afl. It is an accepted 
maxim that the Bank and the aggrieved party should be 
deemed to know 'the law of the land. They cannot plead 
ignorance of law. It 's impossible to conceive that the Bank 
had either the intention or the authority to appoint the De¬ 
posit Collector as an employee of the Bank in the face of 
the taboo provided by Section 10 of the Banking Regula¬ 
tion Act. I have no' hesitation to conclude that there is no 
lelationship of master and servant between the Respondent-- 
Bank and the aggrieved party. The order of termination 
Ex. W-1 merely states that the agency of the Petitioner as 
Deposit Collector stands terminated with immediate effect. 
Ex. M-7 under clause (4) conlemplaies the termination of 
the agency in case the Denosit Collector commits breach of

Rules and RegUfiations or directions. The Management-Bank

the- matter of remittances of the anxmnts collected from the 
depo'hors. Therefare the termination of the agenev is in 
accordance w'th the terms of the agreement Ex. M-7. Even 
if the term.ination of the agency is not in accordance with 
the terms, that is a matter to be agitated in some other

against the Union. 

(16) In the result, I hold that the Union espousing the

not entitled to get anv rei’cf in this dispute liom the Res¬

order as to costs.
